newsitem.title: UK: BA rival Virgin cries foul over Heathrow terminal 5.
newsitem.headline: BA rival Virgin cries foul over Heathrow terminal 5.

text.p: British Airways Plc's arch rival Virgin Atlantic Airways said on Thursday it would challenge a decision giving BA and its prospective alliance partner American Airlines pride of place in London Heathrow's new fifth terminal.

Virgin said it would now make the terminal an issue at the current investigations into BA's proposed alliance with American. The British, U.S. and European Commission's competition authorities are all weighing up whether or not to approve the controversial deal.
"One has got to ask whether this decision is a fair opportunity for Heathrow airport consumers," Virgin's owner Richard Branson said in a statement.
"The idea of giving a brand spanking new facility to one dominant, monopolist, when all the airlines are paying for it (in airport charges) is ridiculous," he said.

"In any other industry such an agreement would be considered outrageous and we intend to pursue this issue during the continuing investigation by (Britain's) Office of Fair Trading and their counterparts in Europe and the U.S." Airport operator BAA Plc announced earlier that it had agreed that BA and its alliance partners should occupy the new terminal if the 1.5 billion pound ($2.4 billion) project wins planning permission.
It says terminal five would allow it to increase capacity gradually at the airport by about 30 million passengers a year to over 80 million by the year 2013.
BAA said it had picked BA to occupy the new terminal following "extensive consultations" with other airlines, including Virgin. "Yes, they were consulted," a company spokesman said.

"But of course, it is not possible to give everybody exactly what they want," he said. "All the airlines were consulted and they received prior warning of what we announced today...about three weeks ago."

BAA said the agreement with BA was conditional upon Heathrow's biggest airline vacating Terminal One which it was proposing to give over to the alliance involving United Airlines, SAS, Air Canada and Thai Airways.
Industry sources said that rival airlines suspected the offer was designed to soften United's opposition to the BA and American deal in Britain and the United States.
But a United spokesman said on Thursday that it would not comment until it had a better idea of what was on offer and whether the facilities at Terminal One would be adequate.
"We are declining comment until we can study the offer futher," said a local spokesman for the airline.

The plan to build the fifth terminal is still subject to planning permission. A public inquiry opened in May 1995 but fierce opposition led by environmental groups, local authorities and some residents means that the inspectors will not finish their work until mid-1998.
BAA said on Thursday that it now hopes to be able to open the first phase of the development in the year 2004, two years later than planned.
Last year, Heathrow handled nearly 56 million passengers but BAA and its airlines say the airport is now close to full capacity.
"It has long been our dream to offer Heathrow customers all our services under one roof," said BA chief executive Bob Ayling in reaction to Thursday's news.
